source.title: The double descent and Runge phenomena in overparametrized polynomial interpolation

record.tranche_reason: The study gives theoretical and numerical results on overparameterized polynomial interpolation that refine the general double-descent claim: outcomes depend on basis and coefficient regularization, and the authors do not establish a general descent past the interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The study tests polynomial degree and interpolation error, not deep-network size, epochs, or increasing sample size. Results cited from other work and the companion article are not extracted. Rows below record the study's own theorems and numerical findings; several plotted outcomes have no reported numerical error values.
record.test_reason: The study's own theorems and numerical examples bear on V4 in a non-network model class, one-dimensional polynomial interpolation. They show whether risk improves past the interpolation threshold depends on basis and coefficient regularizer. The Chebyshev ℓ2 descent ends at a suboptimal limit, and some monomial interpolants get worse than the Lagrange polynomial. No deep-network, epoch, sample-sweep, noise or effective-complexity analysis is included.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add three points. In the Chebyshev ℓ2 case, the authors say a Runge-type target gives a true double descent, but one descending to a suboptimal value worse than a constant fit. They show numerically that overparameterized monomial interpolants can fail where the Lagrange polynomial converges. They do not prove that overparameterization beats the Lagrange polynomial in general.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes one-dimensional polynomial interpolation with minimum coefficient norms, rather than deep-network size sweeps or neural-network test-error measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on the polynomial basis, coefficient norm, target-function class, and sampling points. The study contrasts monomial ℓ1 and ℓ2, Chebyshev ℓ2, and partial Legendre/monomial ℓ2 analyses.
record.problems: Several numerical outcomes are qualitative plots without reported error values. The authors explicitly leave the Legendre-basis conclusion partly conjectural, do not prove that overparameterized solutions outperform Lagrange interpolation generally, and do not establish a general risk curve across polynomial degree.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the Legendre-basis conjecture or the monomial-basis ℓ2 Hardy-space discussion: these are not reported as a direct measured degree-wise test-error result. Figure 7 and Figure 8 examples are also omitted because their text descriptions do not report a degree-wise test-error comparison relevant to V4.

untested.parts: No neural networks; only polynomial degree.
No finite sweep over sample count near the threshold. Only the asymptotic non-commuting limits in n and d.
No measured risk curve across degree, including the threshold. One-dimensional polynomials only; no other model classes.
No effective-complexity predictor of peak location.
No label noise, multiple peaks, or tuned-regularization sweep.
No re-expression against an effective parameter count. The coefficient-norm to function-norm correspondence is discussed but not tested.

missing.what: Non-commutation of limits: lim_d lim_n error = 0 but lim_n lim_d error = ‖f‖ for Chebyshev ℓ2. This bears on V4 and on how sample size interacts with heavy overparameterization.
Figure 6: Chebyshev and Legendre ℓ2 interpolants of f=1 tend toward zero as degree rises to 2000, with Legendre much slower. This is degree-wise evidence on the Legendre basis.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 1 (double descent with a scaled Chebyshev basis) reports results of the companion article [WW26], so it is not recorded as this study's own result. None of the originals is this study. All numerical V4 evidence is qualitative, figure plus caption; there are no error values. The reader's limits_scope label based on R3 is dropped, because R3 cannot show the threshold comparison.

versions.untested_parts: The claim is specifically about deep networks; this study uses polynomial interpolants.
No test-error sweep over training sample count near an interpolation threshold.

The study considers one-dimensional polynomial interpolation and does not establish a general curve across model classes. It does not systematically measure risk across capacity, especially immediately around the interpolation threshold.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
No label-noise or variance sweep, multiple-peak analysis, or optimally tuned regularization test.
The study does not re-express results using an effective parameter count or test whether this converts double descent to an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Chebyshev basis, ℓ2-minimal coefficient interpolant
rows.operation_detail: Theorem establishes the limit of the minimum-coefficient-norm interpolant as polynomial degree tends to infinity.
rows.measure: L2(−1,1) discrepancy from the target, for fixed labels
rows.value: lim_{d→∞} ∥Pd∥L2(−1,1) = 0; for labels yi = f(xi), lim_{d→∞} ∥f − Pd∥L2(−1,1) = ∥f∥L2(−1,1)
rows.note: The limit is the zero function, not necessarily a better approximation than lower-degree solutions. The theorem gives an asymptotic risk value, not a measured fall-rise-fall curve.
rows.check: State kept. The theorem gives only the d→∞ limit (zero function, error ‖f‖), not a curve. The authors call this a descent 'to a suboptimal value'.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine. The theorem establishes Pd → 0 and discrepancy → ‖f‖; arbitrary fixed labels do not establish post-threshold improvement.
source_check.problem: An asymptotic endpoint alone does not establish a partial double-descent effect.

rows.subject: Chebyshev basis, degree-zero least-squares polynomial
rows.operation_detail: The study compares the empirical-mean constant predictor with the limiting high-degree interpolant under a stated condition.

conditions.value: Chebyshev basis; high-degree coefficient ℓ2-minimal interpolants

rows.value: Under the stated condition, ∥f − P0∥L2(−1,1) < lim_{d→∞} ∥f − Pd∥L2(−1,1)
rows.note: This is a conditional comparison with the degree-zero predictor. The authors say that for a Runge-type function this indicates double descent if the error at the interpolation threshold is large, but do not provide that threshold comparison in the corollary.
rows.check: This is a comparator, not a degree sweep. It shows the degree-0 fit beats the overparameterized limit. The threshold error being large is asserted for Runge-type f, not computed here.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine. Under the stated mean condition, the constant empirical-mean predictor has smaller discrepancy than the infinite-degree limit; the condition alone does not establish a peak or subsequent improvement.
source_check.problem: The conditional endpoint comparison cannot establish the degree-dependent effect.

rows.subject: Monomial basis, ℓ1-minimal coefficient interpolant
rows.operation_detail: Theorem bounds interpolation error as degree tends to infinity for ℓ1-minimal monomial coefficients.

conditions.value: absolutely monotonic analytic power series with non-negative coefficients
non-negative sample points including 0 and 1, with xi − xi−1 < K/n; or balanced data

rows.measure: L1 or L∞ discrepancy from f
rows.value: lim_{d→∞} sup_{b∈Md} ∥f − Pb∥L1(0,1) ≤ K(f(b) − f(a))/n; additional L∞ bounds are stated in Theorem 2.1
rows.note: The result bounds high-degree error for a restrictive target-function class. The authors explicitly note that it does not describe an initial ascent and that the error may decrease monotonically; it does not compare high degree with the interpolation-threshold solution.
rows.check: State kept. It bounds high-degree error only. The authors say it shows no initial ascent and no comparison with the Lagrange interpolant, so it cannot show a second descent.
